explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. The writer says believers have “…confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus,” (Hebrews 10:19). Confidence is the key word. He doesn't say "sneak in" or "tiptoe in." He says walk in like you were invited.

Nice guess, but Eden never comes up here. The writer says the place is the Most Holy Place. He says believers have confidence to enter it by the blood of Jesus. So you're still holding a good map, friend, just for a different spot.

Mount Sinai is a big mountain, but the writer never mentions it in this passage. The place he names is the Most Holy Place. Believers have confidence to enter it, he says, by the blood of Jesus (Hebrews 10:19). That's the place on this card.
Yes, baker! The writer says the confidence comes “…by the blood of Jesus,” (Hebrews 10:19). Nothing is added to it. Nobody has to bring a résumé to the door.

The law of Moses does show up later in this passage, but not as the way in. Moses was Israel's leader, and the writer mentions his law in verse 28 for a different reason. For entering the Most Holy Place, he says it's by the blood of Jesus (Hebrews 10:19).

Good works are great, but they aren't what the writer points to here. He says they can enter the Most Holy Place with confidence by the blood of Jesus. The way in comes from Jesus, not from anybody's checklist. That's good news for those of us who still burn the first batch.

True! The writer says it's “the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body,” (Hebrews 10:20). The way is new, it's living, and it's already opened for us. Nobody has to go find a crowbar.

This one is actually true. The writer says the way is “the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body,” (Hebrews 10:20). So it was opened for us through the curtain of Jesus' body. It's easy to second-guess a card like this, friend. I've done it with a timer that was right the whole time.
Right, baker. The writer says “…we have a great priest over the house of God,” (Hebrews 10:21). He uses "great" on purpose. That's a big title, and he doesn't mumble it.

A king is a fine thing to be, but that's not the word the writer uses here. He says believers have a great priest over the house of God (Hebrews 10:21). Hold onto that word, because the next verse builds on it.

Prophets matter in the Bible, but the writer doesn't use that word here. He says “…we have a great priest over the house of God,” (Hebrews 10:21). It's priest, friend. The next verse tells believers what to do because of it.
Yes! After the open way and the great priest, he says, “let us draw near…” (Hebrews 10:22). Notice it's "us." He's walking up with them, not pointing from the back of the room.

The writer says the opposite. With the way opened and a great priest over the house of God, he says, “let us draw near…” (Hebrews 10:22). Standing far off would be like baking a whole batch and eating none of it. Nobody wants that, friend.
Waiting outside is a good plan for a bus, but it's not what the writer says. He says, “let us draw near…” (Hebrews 10:22). The door's been opened for them, so the invitation is to come closer.

That's it, baker. The writer says their hearts are sprinkled “to cleanse us from a guilty conscience…” (Hebrews 10:22). That's the cleaning job. And it's done on the inside, where it's hardest to scrub.
No sickness is mentioned here. The writer says the hearts were sprinkled to cleanse them from a guilty conscience (Hebrews 10:22). It's the guilty feeling inside that gets cleaned.

I wish somebody would sprinkle my bills clean, friend, but that's not what the writer says. The hearts are sprinkled “to cleanse us from a guilty conscience…” (Hebrews 10:22). Debt isn't mentioned in this verse.
True! The writer says, “…our bodies washed with pure water.” (Hebrews 10:22). So it's two things together: hearts sprinkled and bodies washed. Clean inside and clean outside.

That one's actually true. Right after the hearts, the writer says “…and our bodies washed with pure water.” (Hebrews 10:22). Hearts sprinkled, bodies washed. Don't feel bad, friend. Plenty of folks skim right past the second half of a verse.

You got it, baker. The writer says, “…for He who promised is faithful.” (Hebrews 10:23). The grip is tight because of who made the promise. The hope doesn't hang on how strong the one holding it feels today.

The writer doesn't point to their hearts here. He gives the reason in the same verse: “…for He who promised is faithful.” (Hebrews 10:23). The reason is the One who promised. That's a sturdier thing to hold than my own mood on a Monday.

explanations.answer: Their leaders keep watch over them
explanations.explanation: Leaders aren't the reason given in this verse. The writer says they can hold on “…for He who promised is faithful.” (Hebrews 10:23). The reason is the One who made the promise. That's the whole answer, friend.

Yes, baker. The writer says, “And let us consider how to spur one another on to love and good deeds.” (Hebrews 10:24). So the spurring points somewhere good. And you'll notice he says "one another," so everybody gets a turn.
Nope, friend, nothing about wealth or success here. The writer says to spur one another on to love and good deeds (Hebrews 10:24). That's the finish line he sets.
Fame and honor aren't what he's after. The writer says, “…spur one another on to love and good deeds.” (Hebrews 10:24). No spotlight needed. A good deed done quietly counts just as much.

That's it. The writer says, “Let us not neglect meeting together, as some have made a habit…” (Hebrews 10:25). A habit is something you keep doing without thinking. He wants believers to keep showing up instead.
Arguing over the law isn't what he warns about here. He says, “Let us not neglect meeting together, as some have made a habit…” (Hebrews 10:25). The habit is skipping the gathering, friend.
Money isn't mentioned in this warning. The writer says some had made a habit of neglecting meeting together (Hebrews 10:25). That's the habit he names.

It's the other way around, friend. The writer says, “…but let us encourage one another, and all the more as you see the Day approaching.” (Hebrews 10:25). All the more, not less. When the Day gets closer, the encouragement goes up.

Right, baker. The writer says, “…but let us encourage one another, and all the more as you see the Day approaching.” (Hebrews 10:25). All the more! That's the same reason my ovens stay ready. I'm not guessing when the Day is, and the writer doesn't either.

Yes. The writer says that if we deliberately go on sinning after receiving the knowledge of the truth, “…no further sacrifice for sins remains,” (Hebrews 10:26). It's a serious verse, friend. I think it's meant to make us take it seriously.

A city isn't mentioned in this verse. The writer says that no further sacrifice for sins remains for someone who deliberately goes on sinning after receiving the knowledge of the truth (Hebrews 10:26). I think this verse is easier to take in slowly.

Land isn't mentioned here. The writer says “…no further sacrifice for sins remains,” (Hebrews 10:26). That's the thing he says no longer remains. It's a heavy verse, so no worries about reading it twice.

True. The writer says what's left is “…only a fearful expectation of judgment and of raging fire that will consume all adversaries.” (Hebrews 10:27). It's strong language. I think he wants it to land.

This one is true, friend. The writer says what remains is “…only a fearful expectation of judgment and of raging fire that will consume all adversaries.” (Hebrews 10:27). It's a heavy sentence, so it's fair that it takes a second read.

That's what the text says. The writer says, “Anyone who rejected the law of Moses died without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses.” (Hebrews 10:28). I think this one hurts. It's here so the next verse can ask its question.

A fine isn't what the verse says. The writer says anyone who rejected the law of Moses “died without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses.” (Hebrews 10:28). I think this is a hard one to read, friend.
Being sent away isn't what he says. The text says they “died without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses.” (Hebrews 10:28). It's a heavy verse, and I think it's okay to feel that.

Yes, baker. The writer says this person “…has trampled on the Son of God, profaned the blood of the covenant that sanctified him, and insulted the Spirit of grace.” (Hebrews 10:29). The blood of the covenant is the blood of Jesus, which the passage began with in verse 19. It's serious business, friend.

The ark isn't the word here. The writer says the person “…profaned the blood of the covenant that sanctified him…” (Hebrews 10:29). It's the blood of the covenant. Holy things deserve to be handled with care, and so does this verse.

A book isn't what the writer names. He says the person “…profaned the blood of the covenant that sanctified him…” (Hebrews 10:29). The blank is blood, friend. It's a weighty verse, so it helps to read it slowly.
That's it. The writer says, “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.” (Hebrews 10:31). He doesn't soften it. I think that's the point of the whole stop.
Small isn't the word. The writer says, “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.” (Hebrews 10:31). Friend, he says fearful, and he means it.
Strange isn't the word he picks. The writer says, “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.” (Hebrews 10:31). Fearful is the word. It's a good one to remember.

explanations.answer: A great conflict in the face of suffering
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The writer says, “…you endured a great conflict in the face of suffering.” (Hebrews 10:32). These folks had been through it. And he reminds them they came through it.

explanations.answer: A long famine across the whole land
explanations.explanation: A famine isn't mentioned here. The writer says that in those early days they “…endured a great conflict in the face of suffering.” (Hebrews 10:32). That's what he asks them to remember, friend.

explanations.answer: A hard march through the desert
explanations.explanation: A desert march isn't in this verse. The writer says they “…endured a great conflict in the face of suffering.” (Hebrews 10:32). That's the hard stretch he asks them to look back on.

It's the opposite, friend. The writer says, “Sometimes you were publicly exposed to ridicule and persecution…” (Hebrews 10:33). So they weren't kept safe from it. They were out in the open, and they stuck together anyway.

Right, baker. The writer says, “Sometimes you were publicly exposed to ridicule and persecution; at other times you were partners with those who were so treated.” (Hebrews 10:33). So it happened to them, and they also stood beside others it happened to. That's a lot of loyalty.
Joyfully! The writer says they “…joyfully accepted the confiscation of your property…” (Hebrews 10:34). That's not how most of us handle losing a parking spot. Next card tells you why.
Angry is a normal guess, friend. But the writer says they “joyfully accepted the confiscation of your property…” (Hebrews 10:34). Joyfully is the word he uses.
Fearful would make sense to most of us, but that's not the word. The writer says they “joyfully accepted the confiscation of your property…” (Hebrews 10:34). The next card gives the reason he states.

explanations.answer: They had a better and permanent possession
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The writer says they accepted it joyfully, “…knowing that you yourselves had a better and permanent possession.” (Hebrews 10:34). The knowing is what carried them. They held something that couldn't be taken.

explanations.answer: They expected to get it all back soon
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. The writer says they accepted it joyfully “…knowing that you yourselves had a better and permanent possession.” (Hebrews 10:34). The reason is the better possession, not getting things back.

explanations.answer: They never cared much about their things
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that either, friend. It says they accepted it joyfully, “…knowing that you yourselves had a better and permanent possession.” (Hebrews 10:34). I think that's a different thing from not caring.
That's it. The writer says, “So do not throw away your confidence; it holds a great reward.” (Hebrews 10:35). Don't toss it, friend. There's something good inside.
Not a burden, friend. The writer says, “So do not throw away your confidence; it holds a great reward.” (Hebrews 10:35). It's a reward.
No danger is mentioned. The writer says, “So do not throw away your confidence; it holds a great reward.” (Hebrews 10:35). That's a better thing to find in a box.

Yes, baker. The writer says, “You need to persevere, so that after you have done the will of God, you will receive what He has promised.” (Hebrews 10:36). Perseverance means sticking with it. Like waiting for dough to finish rising.

Rest is a good thing, but that's not the word here. The writer says, “You need to persevere, so that after you have done the will of God, you will receive what He has promised.” (Hebrews 10:36). It's persevere, friend.

Repent isn't the word in this verse. The writer says, “You need to persevere, so that after you have done the will of God, you will receive what He has promised.” (Hebrews 10:36). The blank is persevere, friend.
Yes! The quote says, “But My righteous one will live by faith…” (Hebrews 10:38). By faith. That's the way he lives.
Strength isn't what the quote names. It says, “But My righteous one will live by faith…” (Hebrews 10:38). Faith is the word, friend, and a good thing to keep close.
The law is mentioned earlier in the passage, but not here. The quote says, “But My righteous one will live by faith…” (Hebrews 10:38). So the righteous one lives by faith.
True. The quote says, “…and if he shrinks back, I will take no pleasure in him.” (Hebrews 10:38). It's a sober line. I think it's here to help us hold on.
This one's true, friend. The quote says, “…and if he shrinks back, I will take no pleasure in him.” (Hebrews 10:38). It's a sober line, so it makes sense to read it twice.

explanations.answer: Those who have faith and preserve their souls
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The writer says, “But we are not of those who shrink back and are destroyed, but of those who have faith and preserve their souls.” (Hebrews 10:39). Notice the "we." He puts himself in the same group as his readers.

explanations.answer: Those who shrink back and are destroyed
explanations.explanation: He says the opposite. The writer says, “But we are not of those who shrink back and are destroyed, but of those who have faith and preserve their souls.” (Hebrews 10:39). He says "we are not" of that group, friend.

explanations.answer: Those still deciding which way to go
explanations.explanation: He doesn't name a group like that. The writer says, “But we are not of those who shrink back and are destroyed, but of those who have faith and preserve their souls.” (Hebrews 10:39). He puts himself and his readers with those who have faith.
